claims.text: Substitutional alloying with elements of varying atomic radii can introduce controlled lattice distortion in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Controlled lattice distortion introduced through substitutional alloying can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.
Moderate lattice distortion can be introduced without compromising alloy stability or forming unwanted precipitates if suitable alloying elements are selected.
Temperature and cooling rate can be optimized to retain the desired microstructure after substitutional alloying.
Lattice distortion can lead to the formation of defects such as dislocations.
Introduced dislocations can interact with one another and with the alloy microstructure.
Lattice distortion increases strength by providing additional obstacles to dislocation motion.
A controlled population of defects enhances ductility by enabling more efficient plastic deformation mechanisms.
The intervention is expected to increase yield strength by at least 10% relative to the baseline alloy.
The intervention is expected to improve ductility by at least 15% relative to the baseline alloy.
The hypothesized effect should hold for eutectic high-entropy alloys having moderate to high entropy of mixing.
The hypothesized effect should hold at temperatures and strain rates relevant to structural applications.
